name: Prophy paste polish

lead: Prophy paste is an abrasive polishing paste applied by a dental professional with a rotating rubber cup during a cleaning. It removes surface stain and plaque, leaving teeth looking cleaner and smoother.

Fine abrasive particles in the paste are spun against the tooth to polish the surface and lift deposits. It works on external stain rather than the tooth's inner colour. Available research is mostly laboratory work on restorative materials, porcelain and implant surfaces; no cosmetic trial of stain removal was found.

paras: It is part of a professional dental cleaning appointment, applied by a hygienist or dentist.
Lab studies show polishing pastes can change the roughness and gloss of composite resin restorations. It is a professional procedure.

angle.text: A gritty paste polishes the enamel and lifts surface stain, so teeth look cleaner and brighter right after a cleaning. Research on it focuses on abrasivity and dental materials rather than cosmetic results.

lead: Prophy paste is a gritty polishing paste applied with a rotating rubber cup, usually by a dental professional during a cleaning, to polish tooth surfaces and remove some surface deposits.[1][2] It is relevant to appearance because it is used on extrinsic (surface) stain.
The available research examines the paste mostly in the laboratory, for its effects on restorative materials, porcelain and implant surfaces, rather than as a cosmetic whitening treatment in people.

paras: Dental researchers have described rubber-cup prophylaxis with pastes alongside other cleaning instruments, and one study compared prophy paste with ultrasonic and hand instruments on implant abutments.[2] Pastes have also been tested for cleaning cut dentine, where flour of pumice or a prophylaxis paste with a rubber cup was effective at removing the smear layer.[3] A review of mechanical plaque control places professional care as a supplement to daily self-care.[1]

No studies found testing prophy paste as a cosmetic stain-removal or whitening treatment in people. Related work: a clinical study compared sealant retention after two tooth-cleaning techniques, and another compared prophylaxis with toothbrushing before fluoride application.[4][5] A trial examined desensitising agents on dentine hypersensitivity.[6] Laboratory studies tested how polishing pastes change roughness and gloss of composite resin and CAD/CAM composite and how polishing affects dental porcelain.[7][8][9]
Laboratory findings indicate that polishing pastes can change the surface roughness of resin composite materials, which is why their effect on restorations has been studied.[7][8]
